question: Ms. Reyes is planning a two-week unit that introduces about forty new words for food and cooking. She wants her students to still know the words at the end of the term, not only at the end of the week. Her draft plan presents all forty words in the first two lessons through picture-and-translation slides, then moves on to other content and expects students to review the lists at home. Drawing on what the course teaches about how vocabulary is learned and how lessons are planned, what should Ms. Reyes change about her plan, and why?
answer: Ms. Reyes's draft relies on the two weakest methods the vocabulary research identifies: massed presentation of all forty words at once, followed by re-reading the lists at home. Both run against the evidence. On the study-versus-retrieval question, Karpicke and Roediger (2008) demonstrated that once a learner has recalled a word correctly once, further study of that word produces no measurable gain, while further retrieval keeps strengthening it; re-reading a list at home is exactly the low-value re-study the finding warns against. On the timing question, spaced practice reliably beats massed practice: Nakata (2015) found spaced conditions produced stronger retention than massed ones, and Kim and Webb (2022), in a meta-analysis of 48 experiments with 3,411 participants, confirmed a positive effect of spacing across a wide range of learners. Presenting all forty words in the first two lessons and then leaving them behind is massed learning with no planned retrieval. The planning fix follows directly. Ms. Reyes should introduce the words in smaller batches and build short, spaced retrieval events into the plan across the full two weeks and beyond, rather than front-loading presentation and delegating review to unstructured home study. A lesson plan states what learners will be able to do by the end and protects time for it, so the review is written into the sequence as deliberate quizzing, pair testing, and quick production tasks that recur on later days, not added only if time permits. The principle to state plainly is that retrieval spread over time, planned as part of the unit, is what turns forty new words at the end of the week into forty known words at the end of the term.
anchor: Karpicke and Roediger (2008) demonstrated that once a learner has recalled a word correctly once, further study of that word produces no measurable gain in retention at one week, while further retrieval continues to strengthen it.
rubric: Rubric (10 points): identifies that the draft uses massed presentation plus re-reading, the weak approach the evidence argues against (2); cites the retrieval-over-restudy finding, Karpicke and Roediger 2008 (2); cites the spacing-over-massing evidence, Nakata 2015 and/or Kim and Webb 2022 (2); gives a concrete planning fix, spaced retrieval events built into the unit plan rather than left to home study (3); coherent answer that connects the vocabulary evidence to the planning decision (1).
